title: Bodybuilders can't FIGHT (but martial artists should lift)
summary: Part one of NH's martial-arts series lays out his philosophy for programming lifting for fighters: lifting complements but never replaces skill training, hypertrophy builds purposeful muscle as potential that carries over to fighting (not vice versa), and sessions must be short, infrequent, safe and conditioning-heavy. He splits fighters into purists and hybrids and warns against copying drug-fuelled MMA training.
claims: Boxing/savate purist template: Day A dips or weighted push-ups 3x6-8 + calf raises; seal or incline DB rows 4x8-12 + landmine twists; leg press or hack squats 4x10-15 + hang clean pulls. Day B hang power cleans 4x4-8 + neck work; good mornings or deficit deadlifts 3x6-10 + weighted chins 3x5; OHP 4x6-12 + split-stance landmine RDL + grippers. Day C 3-5x3 min dashes plus bodyweight work
He has no fighting credentials: he did martial arts in the past but never at a high level, so he only speaks to building muscle and strength that carries over
Lifting alone does not make you a better fighter: ten years in the gym loses to two years of boxing or BJJ, and a BJJ blue belt would beat him even if he outweighed him by 50 lb
The more skilled the opponent, the less brute force matters; to get better at fighting you must train fighting, and lifting is only a complement

Purists (fighting first) get two minimal, intense lifting sessions a week plus an optional conditioning day; hybrids who want both can repeat the days 3-4 times a week but should rotate exercise variations
Fighters should build purposeful muscles only: every exercise must train a muscle used in the sport, so most isolation work is cut
The idea that weights make fighters too bulky or slow is a myth that still holds back many coaches and senseis, especially in traditional arts like karate and judo
Loading fight movements (dumbbell uppercuts, punching with bands) is misguided; lifting should train muscles in patterns your coach does not already use
Muscle is potential: specificity matters only to a degree, and a biceps built with curls can still pull on a belt or gi
Carryover runs one way: hypertrophy training transfers to fighting, but fight training (e.g. shadowboxing) does nothing for size
Any hour spent lifting is an hour not spent on skill, so his fighter programs take about three hours a week, roughly 1.5 hours per session twice weekly
Place sessions around sparring: don't lift the day before a hard sparring session; recover first and train when fresh
Many top MMA fighters look the way they do because of drugs, not their training; when USADA testing arrived many lost their size
Good fighters on drugs giving hypertrophy advice is usually nonsense, and gimmicks like one-legged bosu-ball uppercuts tend to come from enhanced athletes who grow regardless
Natural fighters must follow strict, orthodox, basic training for years: break down muscle, recover, repeat
Steroids are essentially injectable volume and tonnage, giving free muscle growth on top of the same training
You must choose between being really jacked and being a good fighter; you cannot maximise both
Fighters should track performance first: his programs are low-volume and intense, so strength progression (adding load) drives tonnage
He uses supersets both to save time and to tax the cardiovascular system, since a fighter without cardio is a sitting duck
Conditioning days are deliberately short, brutal and stressful, to replicate the short intense bursts of a fight
If the new lifting fatigue degrades your sparring, cut the lifting back; work capacity improves only with time
Fighting is mostly skill: unassuming people can beat 99% of the population, while big enhanced bodybuilders are slow, immobile and gas out
PEDs make fighters aggressive, confident and explosive but hurt cardiovascular endurance, so they gas out faster
Unused muscle is a burden for a fighter, needing blood, oxygen and energy; every pound must have a use
Every fighter program includes neck training, done with safe isolation (neck extensions, curls, lateral raises) rather than bridges
Fighters should keep one or two reps in reserve and never grind; getting hurt in the gym is the stupidest thing a fighter can do
One-rep-max testing makes no sense for fighters: a max is a grind, not explosive; higher reps build endurance muscle and lower injury risk
Upper back and traps are a major focus: they absorb punches and kicks and contribute to punching power
Abs get both compound and isolation work for hip rotation and absorbing body blows; forearms are trained for grapplers
Few biceps curls or rear-delt isolations: the aim is to build prime movers, not to maximise hypertrophy
Punching power comes from the floor via hip rotation, so lower-body and glute work is mandatory; boxing programs full of bench press are wrong
The conditioning day is optional, takes 35-40 minutes and creates mostly cardiovascular rather than muscular fatigue, a safer option than a third lifting session
exercises: transfer power from floor to upper body
Hang power cleans or landmine power thruster
Neck extensions, neck curls, side neck raises
safe neck development instead of bridges
